tldr: SMART-LLM is a framework that uses large language models to convert high-level natural language task instructions into executable multi-robot task plans through decomposition, coalition formation, and task allocation.
contributions: A benchmark dataset of 36 high-level instructions across four complexity categories (elemental, simple, compound, complex) in the AI2-THOR simulation platform, with ground truth states and robot utilization metrics
A four-stage LLM-based framework (task decomposition, coalition formation, task allocation, execution) using Pythonic few-shot prompts to generate executable multi-robot task plans
Evaluation of the framework in both simulated (AI2-THOR) and real-world settings
methods: The framework operates in four stages: (1) Task Decomposition — the LLM breaks a high-level instruction into ordered sub-tasks given environment details and robot skills encoded as Python dictionaries; (2) Coalition Formation — the LLM identifies which robots or robot teams can perform each sub-task based on skill matching and constraint handling; (3) Task Allocation — the LLM assigns specific robots or coalitions to sub-tasks and generates executable Python code; (4) Task Execution — an interpreter executes the generated code via API calls to robot skills. Pythonic few-shot prompts with commented examples guide the LLM throughout all stages.
results: The benchmark dataset contains 36 tasks: 6 elemental, 8 simple, 14 compound, and 8 complex. Evaluation was conducted in both the AI2-THOR simulation platform and real-world scenarios, demonstrating promising results for generating multi-robot task plans. The dataset includes ground truth final states and robot transition counts for measuring parallelization effectiveness.
limitations: The paper notes that natural language instructions can be incomplete and ambiguous (e.g., missing implicit steps like turning off lights before watching TV in a dim room), requiring extensive prior knowledge to interpret. Fixed-algorithm traditional methods require substantial code modifications for different tasks, while prior LLM-based methods either require extensive task-specific demonstration data lacking generalizability, are limited to specific tasks, or rely on separate LLMs per robot. The paper does not present detailed quantitative comparison numbers against baselines.
